note: What a decoder must conclude when one lineage presents two continuations, and what a device-key transition must carry to be authorized. Every vector states its expected outcome and validate_lineage_fork_and_rotation in scripts/repository/validate_planning_artifacts.py recomputes it, so a vector cannot record an outcome the stated rules do not produce. The resolution of each forked lineage is additionally built into a packages/schemas/fork-resolution-v1.schema.json record and validated against that schema, so the fixture cannot describe a resolution the normative record has no shape for. This is a fixture. No VibeProof implementation reads it, and passing it is not evidence that a decoder exists.
resolver_rules: A lineage starts at generation 0 with the head token 'genesis' and no bound installation.
An installation reference already bound to a different device forks the lineage at the current tip generation. It is checked first because a copied store presents it before it presents a claim.

A submission whose stated previous head is not a head this lineage ever held is refused with CLAIM_GAP_DECLARATION_REQUIRED. It is refused rather than quarantined: nothing about it identifies a branch.
A submission whose previous head is the current tip and whose sequence is one past the tip generation is accepted and becomes the new tip.
A submission whose previous head is the current tip and whose sequence is anything else is refused with CLAIM_SEQUENCE_UNEXPECTED.

A submission whose previous head is an earlier head of this lineage forks it at that generation. The basis is duplicate-sequence-continuation when the sequence is one the lineage already issued, and divergent-commitment-chain when it is not.

On a fork, every submission already accepted above the fork generation is quarantined retroactively, together with the submission that caused the fork. D-072 quarantines every post-fork branch, including the one that arrived first, so arriving first is not a way to win a fork.
Every submission after a fork is quarantined with CLAIM_CHAIN_FORK, whichever device sent it.
Claims at or below the fork generation stay accepted. A fork says nothing about work already accepted.

Two acknowledged heads in one lineage resolve to the greater sequence, which the server issued; two equal heads are a checkpoint mismatch and fork the lineage. Ordering by arrival time would let a clone with a fast clock win.

lineages.title: One device, one chain, nothing to resolve
lineages.note: The control. Without it every assertion below is satisfied by a resolver that quarantines everything, which is the failure mode a fork corpus invites.

lineages.title: A copied store re-issues a sequence the lineage already used
lineages.note: The case D-592 rekeyed device_sequences to make observable, carried one table further. device-b holds a copy of device-a's store and continues from generation 2 with sequence 3, which device-a has already spent. Both branches lose their post-fork claims; generations 1 and 2 are untouched.

lineages.title: A restored store extends a head the lineage moved past
lineages.note: device-d was restored from a backup taken at generation 1 and continues with a sequence the lineage has not issued. The sequence number alone shows nothing wrong; the commitment head does. The fork is at generation 1, so generation 1 survives and device-c's generations 2 and 3 do not.

lineages.title: Two devices present one installation identity
lineages.note: The clone copied the root installation identity along with everything else, so it is observable before either device submits a conflicting sequence. Detection precedence puts it first for that reason: waiting for the sequence collision would accept one more generation from a store known to be duplicated.

lineages.title: A gap and an out-of-order sequence are refused, not quarantined
lineages.note: Neither identifies a branch, so neither opens a fork case. Without these two the resolver could answer every input with 'quarantined' and still match the corpus.

checkpoint_resolutions.title: A restored device presents an older acknowledged head
checkpoint_resolutions.note: The owner decision is that the newest checkpoint wins. The server issued both sequences, so the ordering is over its own counter and not over either device's clock.

checkpoint_resolutions.title: Two devices acknowledge the same head
checkpoint_resolutions.note: Newest-wins cannot choose between equals, and two receipts at one head inside one lineage are two branches. unique (lineage_id, accepted_through_claim_sequence) on checkpoint_receipts refuses the second write, which is this row expressed as a constraint.

rotations.title: An ordinary rotation carries both key authorizations and the account authorization
The outgoing key did not sign
rotations.note: The continuity half of the pair. Admitting this is admitting a rotation by whoever holds the account session, which is the takeover the pair exists to refuse.

rotations.title: The incoming key did not sign
rotations.note: The control half of the pair. Without it a lineage can be rotated onto a key nobody has demonstrated possession of.

rotations.title: Both keys signed and the account did not re-authenticate
rotations.note: The third gate, at a different layer from the pair. A device that already holds both keys is exactly the position a stolen laptop is in.

rotations.title: Lost-key recovery, authorized by an approved recovery case
rotations.note: The path that cannot produce the outgoing signature, because the key is gone. It is a separate action rather than a rotation with a waiver, so no rotation can be admitted by asserting a recovery.

rotations.title: A recovery still inside its cooling-off window
A recovery presenting an outgoing-key signature
rotations.note: A rotation wearing a recovery's authorization. If the outgoing key can sign, the key is not lost and the ordinary path applies; admitting this makes the recovery authority reachable without losing anything.

rotations.title: A rotation carrying a recovery approval
rotations.note: The mirror image. A recovery approval on a rotation row is a second authority for one act, and the one that would be reached for when a key signature is missing.

rotations.title: First enrolment, which has no predecessor to sign
An enrolment naming a previous key
rotations.note: An enrolment that has a predecessor is a rotation, and calling it an enrolment is how a rotation avoids needing the outgoing key's signature.

rotations.title: Revoking a key the participant may no longer hold
rotations.note: The one action that installs no key and therefore proves control of none. Requiring a key signature here would make a lost key unrevokable, which is the situation revocation exists for.

rotations.title: A revocation nobody re-authenticated for
rotations.note: Revocation is the only path with no key authorization at all, so the account authorization is the only thing standing between a stale session and cutting a competitor's device out of its lineage.
